subChunks.title: Microbiology & Virology — The Invisible Kingdom

storyBeats.txt: Theodora held up a glass of water. "There are more bacterial cells in the human body than human cells — ten times as many, by some estimates. Most are essential: the gut microbiome digests fibres we cannot process ourselves, synthesises vitamins, trains the immune system. The microbial world did not invade us. We evolved inside it, and we depend on it."

"Until the 1670s, the microscopic world was invisible and unsuspected. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground lenses of extraordinary quality and peered into pond water, seeing what he called 'animalcules' — living creatures of unimaginable smallness. The microbial world opened to human sight, and medicine was never the same."

"Viruses are stranger still — not cells, not quite alive by some definitions, yet responsible for plagues that have reshaped human history. Smallpox killed perhaps 300 million people in the 20th century alone. Influenza killed 50–100 million in 1918 in months. COVID-19 reached every inhabited landmass in weeks. Understanding how viruses replicate, evolve, and evade immunity is not an academic exercise. It is the foundation of pandemic preparedness."

subChunks.hookHtml: Microbiology encompasses the study of organisms invisible to the naked eye — bacteria, archaea, fungi, protozoa, and algae — as well as the acellular agents of disease: viruses, viroids, and prions. Microorganisms were the first life forms on Earth (≈3.5 billion years ago) and remain the most abundant and metabolically diverse forms of life. They drive global biogeochemical cycles, underpin agriculture and food production, cause infectious diseases, and are increasingly exploited in medicine and biotechnology. Virology — the study of viruses — sits at the boundary of biology and chemistry, raising fundamental questions about the nature of life.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Microbial World — Domains and Diversity

Bacteria: Prokaryotes — no membrane-bound nucleus, circular DNA, ribosomes (70S). Cell walls typically contain peptidoglycan. Gram stain distinguishes: Gram-positive (thick peptidoglycan wall, stains purple) and Gram-negative (thin wall + outer lipopolysaccharide membrane, stains pink) — clinically important because it predicts antibiotic sensitivity.

Archaea: Prokaryotes superficially similar to bacteria but with distinct biochemistry — different cell membrane lipids (ether-linked), no peptidoglycan. Many are extremophiles (hyperthermophiles, halophiles, methanogens). Evolutionarily more closely related to eukaryotes than to bacteria.

Eukaryotic microbes: Fungi (moulds and yeasts — cell walls of chitin; cause athlete's foot, thrush, serious systemic infections in immunocompromised patients). Protozoa (single-celled eukaryotes; Plasmodium causes malaria; Giardia, Trypanosoma). Algae (photosynthetic; form basis of marine food webs; some produce toxins — harmful algal blooms).

Bacterial Growth and Reproduction

Bacteria reproduce by binary fission — exponential growth under ideal conditions. Growth curve: lag phase (adaptation) → exponential (log) phase (rapid doubling) → stationary phase (resource limitation, waste accumulation) → death phase. Doubling time varies: E. coli ≈20 min at 37°C; Mycobacterium tuberculosis ≈15–20 hours. In exponential phase: N = N₀ × 2^(t/g), where g is generation time.

Bacterial metabolism: Extraordinary metabolic diversity. Energy sources: light (phototrophs) or chemicals (chemotrophs). Carbon sources: CO₂ (autotrophs) or organic compounds (heterotrophs). Obligate aerobes (require O₂), obligate anaerobes (killed by O₂), facultative anaerobes (can switch). Nitrogen fixation: some bacteria (Rhizobium, Azotobacter) convert atmospheric N₂ to NH₃ — essential for the nitrogen cycle and crop agriculture.

Viruses — Structure and Replication

Viruses are not cells. They consist of: genetic material (DNA or RNA, single or double-stranded) enclosed in a protein coat (capsid), sometimes surrounded by a lipid envelope (derived from host cell membrane). They have no ribosomes, no metabolic machinery — they can only replicate inside a host cell. Whether viruses are "alive" is a philosophical debate; they are not cellular and cannot reproduce independently.

Viral replication cycle: (1) Attachment — viral surface proteins bind specific receptors on host cell (determines host range and tropism). (2) Entry — injection of nucleic acid (bacteriophages) or endocytosis/fusion (animal viruses). (3) Replication — using host cell machinery to copy viral genome and synthesise viral proteins. (4) Assembly — new viral particles assembled. (5) Release — lysis (bursting the cell) or budding (enveloped viruses). Lytic vs lysogenic cycles in bacteriophages: lysogeny — viral DNA integrates into host genome as a prophage, replicating silently until stress triggers the lytic cycle.

RNA viruses and mutation: RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRp) lack proofreading → very high mutation rates → rapid evolution → vaccine and antiviral escape. Examples: influenza, HIV, SARS-CoV-2, hepatitis C.

Pathogenesis — How Microbes Cause Disease

Bacterial pathogenesis: Mechanisms include: adhesion to host surfaces, invasion of host cells, toxin production (exotoxins — secreted proteins; endotoxins — LPS from Gram-negative outer membrane, triggers septic shock), immune evasion (capsules, intracellular survival).

Koch's Postulates (1884): four criteria for establishing that a specific microorganism causes a specific disease: (1) organism found in all cases; (2) isolated in pure culture; (3) inoculation causes disease in healthy host; (4) organism re-isolated from the diseased host. Now modified for viruses and for organisms that cannot be cultured.

Antimicrobials and Resistance

Antibiotics target features of bacteria absent in eukaryotes: cell wall synthesis (penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin), protein synthesis on 70S ribosomes (aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, macrolides), DNA replication (fluoroquinolones), cell membrane (polymyxins). Antifungals target ergosterol (not present in human membranes). Antivirals target viral-specific proteins (reverse transcriptase, protease, neuraminidase).

Antibiotic resistance mechanisms: Enzymatic inactivation (β-lactamases destroy penicillin ring), efflux pumps (export antibiotic before it acts), target modification (altered penicillin-binding proteins — MRSA), reduced permeability (less drug enters). Resistance genes spread via horizontal gene transfer: plasmids, transposons, bacteriophages. MRSA, MDR-TB, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae are major global health threats.

Beneficial Microorganisms

Gut microbiome: ≈10¹³ bacteria, 1000+ species. Functions: digestion of dietary fibre → short-chain fatty acids (butyrate — colonocyte fuel), vitamin synthesis (K, B12), immune training (tolerance vs pathogen responses), barrier function. Dysbiosis (altered composition) associated with IBD, obesity, mental health disorders. Probiotics and faecal microbiota transplant (FMT) are therapeutic interventions.

Industrial microbiology: Fermentation produces ethanol, cheese, yogurt, bread, antibiotics (penicillin from Penicillium), and recombinant proteins (insulin produced in E. coli). Bioremediation uses microbes to degrade pollutants (oil spills, heavy metals).
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what a virus actually is and why it is so hard to treat viral infections with drugs compared to bacterial infections.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus. It attaches to the ACE2 receptor on human respiratory epithelial cells via its spike protein. (1) Explain what 'positive-sense RNA' means and how this affects the viral replication strategy compared to negative-sense RNA viruses. (2) Why does SARS-CoV-2 have a higher mutation rate than DNA viruses such as herpesviruses? (3) The spike protein is the main target of COVID-19 vaccines. Explain why antibodies to the spike protein can prevent infection. (4) Some SARS-CoV-2 variants (e.g. Omicron) showed significantly reduced vaccine effectiveness against infection. Using evolutionary principles, explain how such immune-escape variants arise. (5) Why was it possible to develop mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 within months, when traditional vaccine development typically takes 10–15 years?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Positive-sense ssRNA has the same sequence as mRNA and can be directly translated by host ribosomes upon entry into the cell — it acts immediately as a template for protein synthesis, including the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) needed to copy the genome. Negative-sense RNA viruses (e.g. influenza) must first use a viral RdRp (packaged in the virion) to transcribe the genome into positive-sense mRNA before translation can begin. Positive-sense RNA viruses can potentially replicate more rapidly because they skip this first step; they also need to package fewer proteins in the virion.

(2) SARS-CoV-2 replicates using RdRp, which lacks the proofreading exonuclease activity of DNA polymerases. Errors introduced during RNA copying are not corrected — leading to a mutation rate ≈10⁶ times higher per base than cellular DNA replication. (Note: SARS-CoV-2 is unusual among RNA viruses in having a proofreading exonuclease — nsp14 — which partially reduces its mutation rate compared to other coronaviruses, but it is still orders of magnitude more error-prone than DNA viruses.) DNA viruses like herpesviruses use (or co-opt) high-fidelity DNA polymerases with proofreading, giving much lower mutation rates and therefore less antigenic variation.

(3) The spike protein mediates attachment to ACE2 and membrane fusion — both essential first steps of infection. Antibodies binding to the spike protein can: (a) Neutralise the virus by physically blocking the RBD (receptor-binding domain) from engaging ACE2 — the virus cannot attach and enter cells. (b) Opsonise virus particles for phagocytosis. (c) Trigger complement-mediated lysis. If sufficient neutralising antibody is present at the site of infection, virus cannot bind host cells and infection is aborted. This is why spike-targeted vaccines protect against infection.

(4) SARS-CoV-2 generates enormous diversity through RdRp errors. Most mutations are deleterious (virus less fit), some neutral, rare ones advantageous. When a large fraction of the population has antibodies to the original spike sequence, variants with mutations in the spike protein's antibody-binding sites have a selective advantage — they are less well recognised by existing antibodies, replicate more efficiently in previously immune hosts, and spread. Omicron had ≈30+ mutations in spike, including many in the ACE2-binding domain and antibody epitopes. Immune-escape variants arise and spread by natural selection in populations with high vaccine or infection-induced immunity — exactly analogous to antibiotic resistance.

(5) mRNA vaccines use the sequence of the viral spike protein (known within weeks of the genome being sequenced in January 2020) to produce lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA. The platform was already developed for oncology and other vaccines — only the mRNA sequence needed to change. Traditional vaccines required: growing attenuated or killed virus (requires containment facilities, time), or producing protein subunits in cell culture (months of scale-up). Safety and efficacy testing timelines were compressed by running phases in parallel (not sequentially), extremely large trial enrolments (faster statistical power), and regulatory rolling review — not by cutting safety corners. The mRNA itself is degraded within days; it does not enter the nucleus or interact with DNA.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Antibiotic resistance is described by the WHO as one of the greatest threats to global health. (1) Explain two distinct biochemical mechanisms by which bacteria can become resistant to penicillin, with a specific example of each. (2) MRSA (Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) has acquired the mecA gene, which encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a). Explain why this mutation confers resistance to virtually all β-lactam antibiotics, not just methicillin. (3) A hospital reduces its antibiotic prescribing by 30%. A microbiologist predicts that antibiotic resistance rates in the hospital will fall over time. Explain the evolutionary mechanism behind this prediction. Under what conditions might this prediction fail? (4) A patient with a urinary tract infection (UTI) is given a 7-day course of antibiotics and feels better after 3 days, so stops taking the tablets. A nurse explains this increases resistance risk. Explain the evolutionary reasoning. (5) Bacteriophage therapy — using viruses that infect bacteria — has been proposed as an alternative to antibiotics. Describe one advantage and one significant challenge of phage therapy.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Two resistance mechanisms: (a) β-lactamase production: bacteria produce enzymes (β-lactamases, including extended-spectrum β-lactamases — ESBLs) that hydrolyse the β-lactam ring of penicillin, inactivating it before it can reach its target. Example: many E. coli strains produce TEM-1 β-lactamase. This is the most common mechanism — overcome by adding β-lactamase inhibitors (clavulanic acid in co-amoxiclav). (b) Efflux pumps: membrane-spanning pump proteins (e.g. MexAB-OprM in Pseudomonas aeruginosa) actively export antibiotics from the bacterial cell before they can reach effective concentrations. Not specific to penicillin; often confer multi-drug resistance by pumping out structurally unrelated antibiotics.

(2) β-lactam antibiotics work by binding to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), which are enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan during cell wall synthesis. The drug mimics the natural substrate, binds covalently to PBP's active site, and irreversibly inhibits it — preventing cell wall synthesis → bacterial lysis. MRSA's mecA-encoded PBP2a has an altered active site with much lower affinity for all β-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) — the structural change is in the binding pocket shared by the entire β-lactam family. PBP2a can still perform peptidoglycan cross-linking (using its own catalytic mechanism), so cell wall synthesis continues despite all β-lactam antibiotics present. This is why the resistance is class-wide, not drug-specific.

(3) Evolutionary mechanism of resistance reduction: Antibiotic resistance genes and mechanisms have fitness costs in the absence of antibiotic pressure — expressing β-lactamases, maintaining efflux pumps, or possessing altered PBPs consumes cellular resources. Without antibiotic selection pressure, susceptible bacteria (no resistance cost) outcompete resistant ones over generations → frequency of resistant bacteria falls. Also: some resistance plasmids are lost without selective maintenance. Prediction may fail if: (a) resistance genes are on plasmids already widespread in the bacterial population and difficult to displace; (b) resistance mutations are cost-free or compensatory mutations have offset the fitness cost; (c) resistance is maintained by co-selection (resistance genes linked on plasmids with genes conferring other advantages — heavy metal resistance, virulence factors); (d) resistant bacteria persist in reservoirs (environment, animals, patients) and recolonise.

(4) Evolutionary reasoning for completing antibiotics: Early in the course, the antibiotic rapidly kills the most susceptible bacteria (those with no resistance mechanisms) — symptoms improve as bacterial load drops. However, a small subpopulation of bacteria with partial resistance or higher tolerance may persist. Stopping early leaves these partially resistant bacteria alive. Without continued antibiotic pressure, they can regrow — but now they make up a larger proportion of the remaining population than they did initially. If the infection recurs, it is enriched with more resistant bacteria. Additionally, sub-therapeutic antibiotic concentrations (as the drug washes out after stopping) apply selection pressure for resistance without killing bacteria effectively — the "mutant selection window." Completing the full course maintains therapeutic levels, killing the pathogen before resistant mutants can proliferate.

(5) Advantage: bacteriophages are highly specific — a phage infects only one or a few bacterial species, leaving commensal flora unharmed. This is in contrast to broad-spectrum antibiotics that disrupt the microbiome. Phages can also evolve alongside bacteria to overcome phage resistance. Challenge: phages are equally susceptible to evolutionary resistance — bacteria develop anti-phage mechanisms (restriction-modification, CRISPR-Cas immune systems, surface receptor loss) rapidly. Phage preparations require careful selection for the specific pathogen (personalised treatment), making standardisation and regulatory approval extremely challenging. The immune system can also neutralise phages, reducing efficacy. Phage therapy remains experimental in most countries, though it has been used successfully in compassionate-use cases.
learningObjectives: Distinguish bacteria, archaea, viruses, and eukaryotic microbes by structure, replication strategy, and metabolic capability.
Describe the lytic viral replication cycle and explain why RNA viruses evolve faster than DNA viruses.
Explain at least three distinct mechanisms of antibiotic resistance and describe how resistance spreads via horizontal gene transfer.
Describe the human gut microbiome and explain how dysbiosis is associated with disease, and how beneficial microorganisms are exploited industrially.
commonMistakes: Treating antibiotics as effective against viruses — antibiotics target bacterial-specific structures (cell walls, 70S ribosomes); viruses use host cell machinery and lack these targets; antiviral drugs target virus-specific proteins.

Thinking individual bacteria become resistant by 'learning' from exposure — resistance arises by random mutation or horizontal gene transfer; antibiotic exposure selects for pre-existing resistant variants, not individual adaptation.

Confusing lytic and lysogenic cycles — lytic cycle immediately destroys the host cell; lysogenic cycle involves integration of viral DNA into the host genome, where it replicates silently until triggered.

Assuming the gut microbiome is simply 'good bacteria' — the microbiome is an ecosystem with complex interactions; its composition varies between individuals, is influenced by diet and antibiotics, and its role in disease is nuanced and still being established.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly describes the five-step viral replication cycle and explains the implications of positive-sense vs negative-sense RNA genomes.
Accurately explains β-lactamase resistance, efflux pump resistance, and target modification, and describes horizontal gene transfer mechanisms.
Explains Koch's Postulates and their limitations for viruses, and describes how viral evolution drives immune escape.
Describes at least two beneficial applications of microorganisms (gut microbiome, industrial fermentation, bioremediation) with mechanistic explanation.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Bacteria have adaptive immune systems: CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) arrays store short sequences from past viral infections. When the same virus attacks again, Cas nucleases use these stored sequences as guides to cut viral DNA. This natural system — discovered in the 2000s and repurposed for genome editing by Doudna and Charpentier (Nobel Prize 2020) — is essentially bacterial immunological memory at the molecular level.

Bacteria communicate by releasing and detecting small signalling molecules (autoinducers) whose concentration reflects population density. When concentration exceeds a threshold (quorum), bacteria alter gene expression collectively — switching on biofilm formation, virulence factor production, or sporulation. Quorum sensing coordinates community behaviour and is a target for new antimicrobial strategies that disrupt bacterial communication rather than killing bacteria directly.

Bacteriophages (phages) are viruses that infect bacteria — the most numerous biological entities on Earth (≈10³¹ estimated). The human gut contains a vast phageome (phage community) that modulates bacterial populations. Phage therapy — using lytic phages to kill pathogenic bacteria — is being revisited as antibiotic resistance grows. Phages are also vectors for horizontal gene transfer (transduction), driving bacterial evolution and resistance spread.

Infectious misfolded proteins — no DNA or RNA. Prion protein (PrP) normally folds correctly; when it misfoldsinto an abnormal conformation (PrPSc), it catalytically converts normal PrP copies to the misfolded form, propagating exponentially. Causes fatal neurodegenerative diseases: CJD, variant CJD (linked to BSE 'mad cow disease'), Kuru, scrapie in sheep. Prusiner won the Nobel Prize in 1997. Prions are extraordinarily resistant to sterilisation — survive autoclaving, radiation, and UV.

Most emerging infectious diseases (70%+) are zoonotic — originating in animal reservoirs and spilling over to humans. HIV from chimpanzees (SIVcpz); SARS-CoV-2 from bats (likely via an intermediate host); Ebola from bats; influenza from birds and pigs. Key risk factors: deforestation (human-wildlife contact), intensive animal farming, live animal markets, international travel. Spillover requires the virus to bind human receptors and replicate in human cells — often requiring only 1–2 mutations in surface proteins.

questions.questionHtml: A bacterium with a doubling time of 20 minutes starts as a single cell. How many bacteria will be present after 3 hours, assuming exponential growth conditions?
questions.explanationHtml: Number of generations in 3 hours (180 minutes) = 180/20 = 9 generations. Number of bacteria = 2⁹ = 512. Formula: N = N₀ × 2^(t/g) = 1 × 2^(180/20) = 2⁹ = 512. This illustrates the explosive potential of bacterial exponential growth — after 24 hours (72 generations): 2⁷² ≈ 4.7 × 10²¹. In practice, resources and waste limit growth to the stationary phase long before these numbers are reached.

questions.questionHtml: HIV is an enveloped retrovirus that uses reverse transcriptase to copy its RNA genome into DNA. Which property of reverse transcriptase makes combination antiretroviral therapy (using multiple drugs simultaneously) so important?
options: Reverse transcriptase is identical to human DNA polymerase, making drug targeting very difficult

Reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading ability, generating high mutation rates that create diverse viral variants; multiple drugs simultaneously target different viral proteins, making the probability of simultaneous resistance mutations extremely low
Reverse transcriptase is only active in CD4+ T cells, limiting where drugs need to reach
Reverse transcriptase mutations always reduce viral fitness, so resistance is self-limiting without drug combinations
questions.correctAnswer: Reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading ability, generating high mutation rates that create diverse viral variants; multiple drugs simultaneously target different viral proteins, making the probability of simultaneous resistance mutations extremely low
questions.explanationHtml: HIV reverse transcriptase lacks 3'→5' proofreading exonuclease activity → error rate ≈3 × 10⁻⁵ per base per replication cycle. With ≈9,700 bases in the HIV genome and ≈10¹⁰ replication cycles per day: virtually every possible single mutation — including drug resistance mutations — exists in the viral population at any moment before treatment starts. A single drug: resistant variants pre-exist and are rapidly selected within weeks. Three drugs targeting different viral proteins (e.g. reverse transcriptase + protease + integrase): the probability of a single virion simultaneously carrying resistance mutations for all three is ≈(10⁻⁵)³ = 10⁻¹⁵ per cycle. At 10¹⁰ cycles/day: expected frequency ≈10⁻⁵ triple-resistant virions per day — effectively never. cART suppresses viral replication below the threshold where triple resistance can evolve.

questions.questionHtml: A doctor prescribes a broad-spectrum antibiotic for a patient with a confirmed viral upper respiratory tract infection ('a cold'), arguing: 'It may not help the cold, but it will prevent secondary bacterial infections.' Evaluate this clinical reasoning.
options: Correct — broad-spectrum antibiotics are standard prophylaxis for all respiratory infections to prevent secondary pneumonia

Incorrect — antibiotics do not treat viral infections; using them prophylactically for secondary bacterial infections is not evidence-based practice, exposes the patient to antibiotic side effects (including C. difficile colitis from microbiome disruption), and contributes to antibiotic resistance without proven benefit
Correct — the risk of secondary bacterial pneumonia in patients with viral URTIs is high enough to justify prophylactic antibiotics in all cases
Incorrect — antibiotics are ineffective against viruses, but prophylactic use is still appropriate to maintain the gut microbiome against viral disruption
questions.correctAnswer: Incorrect — antibiotics do not treat viral infections; using them prophylactically for secondary bacterial infections is not evidence-based practice, exposes the patient to antibiotic side effects (including C. difficile colitis from microbiome disruption), and contributes to antibiotic resistance without proven benefit
questions.explanationHtml: This question combines virology, antibiotic pharmacology, and evidence-based medicine. (1) Antibiotics target bacterial structures absent in viruses — they cannot treat or prevent viral replication. (2) Evidence: systematic reviews and guidelines (WHO, NICE) consistently find that prophylactic antibiotics for uncomplicated viral URTIs do not reduce the incidence of secondary bacterial infections in otherwise healthy patients and are not recommended. (3) Harms: broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt the gut microbiome, creating an ecological vacuum that C. difficile (and other opportunists) can exploit — C. difficile colitis can be life-threatening, especially in elderly patients. Patients also experience antibiotic side effects (allergy, GI disturbance). (4) Systemic harm: each unnecessary prescription selects for resistance in the patient's flora and contributes to the community resistance burden. This is the most common driver of antibiotic overprescribing in primary care and a major target of antimicrobial stewardship programmes. The appropriate management of an uncomplicated viral URTI in a healthy adult is supportive care (rest, fluids, analgesia) with antibiotic review only if symptoms worsen or bacterial superinfection is suspected (fever >3–5 days, purulent sputum, clinical deterioration).
